prompt: By the course's definition, when does a system scale?

choices.text: When the next unit of load costs about what the last one did
choices.why: Right. Scaling is a claim about the cost of more load, not about speed.

choices.text: When it runs on more than one machine, so that the load is divided between them
choices.why: Several machines that all wait for one row scale no better than one.

choices.text: When it is built on a database known for scaling
choices.why: The same database runs systems that scale and systems that do not; the design decides.

choices.text: When each request is answered in under a millisecond, however many users are sending them at once
choices.why: That is speed. A fast program can still fall over at the first thousand users.

prompt: Ten cashiers each take one minute per customer. An eleventh is hired. What happens to the time each customer spends being served?

choices.text: It stays at one minute; throughput is what rises
choices.why: Right. Capacity raises how many are served per hour, not how long one takes.

choices.text: It falls to about 55 seconds
choices.why: Each cashier still takes a minute; the extra one serves other customers in parallel.

choices.text: It falls by a tenth, because the work is divided further
choices.why: One customer's service is not divided between cashiers.

choices.text: It rises, because coordinating eleven cashiers costs time
choices.why: Only if they shared something. Independent cashiers do not coordinate.

prompt: A team makes the part of its system that is not the bottleneck twice as fast. What changes in the measured throughput?

choices.text: It doubles, because half the path is now twice as fast
choices.why: Throughput is set by the bottleneck, not by the average of the path.

choices.text: It falls, because the bottleneck now receives work faster than before
choices.why: A longer queue in front of the bottleneck raises latency; the rate it serves at stays the same.

choices.text: It rises by a quarter, the share that part had of the total time
choices.why: That reasoning is about one request's latency, and even there only if that part was on its path.

choices.text: Nothing measurable
choices.why: Right. The work still waits at the narrowest point, which did not change.

prompt: Why does this course recommend a virtual machine over Docker installed on the computer you use every day?

choices.text: Its processors are yours alone, so you measure the lab
choices.why: Right. The course measures throughput, and anything else running on the processors becomes part of the number.

choices.text: Docker does not run outside a virtual machine
choices.why: Docker Engine runs directly on Linux; the installed path works.

choices.text: A virtual machine is faster than the computer it runs on
choices.why: It cannot be; it uses a share of that computer.

choices.text: The platform provides the virtual machine image
choices.why: The platform provides no machine; you build the lab from an Ubuntu image.

prompt: Why is joining the docker group a reason to prefer a virtual machine for the lab?

choices.text: The group only exists inside virtual machines
choices.why: Installing Docker creates it on any Linux.

choices.text: Membership of that group is as good as root on that machine
choices.why: Right. Whoever can talk to Docker's socket can start a container that mounts the whole disk.

choices.text: Joining it needs a reinstall of the system
choices.why: It needs a new login session, nothing more.

choices.text: It turns off the computer's firewall so that containers can publish their ports
choices.why: The group grants access to Docker's socket; it does nothing to a firewall.

prompt: You edit schema.sql and run docker compose up -d while the db container from before is still there. Why are the old tables still what you see?

choices.text: PostgreSQL caches the schema for a day
choices.why: There is no such cache; the file is simply not read again.

choices.text: The file must be named init.sql
choices.why: Any .sql file in that directory runs, under the empty-directory condition.

choices.text: The image runs files in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d only when the data directory is empty
choices.why: Right. A docker compose down removes the container and its data, and the next up runs the file again.

choices.text: Compose never mounts a file into a container that is already running, so the new version is not seen
choices.why: The file is mounted; it is the entrypoint that ignores it once data exists.

prompt: What is the host field in every answer of the box office for?

choices.text: To sign the ticket
choices.why: The code is computed from the show and the seat only.

choices.text: To identify the database server
choices.why: It is the app container's own name, from socket.gethostname().

choices.text: To tell the client which address to use next time
choices.why: Clients always go through nginx; nothing reads the field to choose an address.

choices.text: To show which copy of the program answered
choices.why: Right. With several copies behind nginx, it is how you see the requests being divided.

prompt: In compose.yaml, the line that caps each copy of the box office at one processor's worth of time is ___: 1.
Right after sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, docker compose up -d still says permission denied. What fixes it?

choices.text: Logging out and in again
choices.why: Right. A session reads its groups when it starts.

choices.text: Running chmod 777 on Docker's socket
choices.why: That would give every user on the machine root through Docker, and the group already solves it.

choices.text: Reinstalling Docker with the group already in place
choices.why: The account is already in the group; only the session does not know.

choices.text: Restarting the Docker daemon
choices.why: The daemon is fine; the user's session lacks the group.

prompt: curl to the box office returns nginx's 502 Bad Gateway, and it does not go away. Where do you look first?

choices.text: At docker compose logs app
choices.why: Right. 502 means the thing behind nginx did not answer, so its log says why.

choices.text: At the port published in compose.yaml
choices.why: The request reached nginx, so the port works.

choices.text: At the load generator's settings
choices.why: curl alone produced it; load.py is not involved.

choices.text: At nginx.conf, since nginx produced the error page
choices.why: nginx is only reporting; the failure is behind it.

prompt: Compose reports a YAML error 'at L3.C3-L20.C4: did not find expected key'. How should you read the location?

choices.text: The file has errors on lines 3 and 20, and the columns say which character to delete on each
choices.why: One misplaced space produced it.

choices.text: Line 3 is wrong
choices.why: Line 3 is where the block starts; in the capture the line with three spaces was further down.

choices.text: Line 20 is wrong, because that is where the parser stopped reading
choices.why: Line 20 is where the parser stopped, past the cause.

choices.text: As a block that failed to parse; the bad line is inside it
choices.why: Right. The parser names the mapping it gave up on, not the guilty line.

prompt: What does a p95 of 196 ms say?

choices.text: Requests took 196 ms at 95% load
choices.why: The 95 is a share of requests, not of load.

choices.text: 5% of the requests failed
choices.why: Failures are in the status line; latency percentiles describe answered requests.

choices.text: 95 out of every 100 requests finished in 196 ms or less
choices.why: Right. The other 5 took longer.

choices.text: The average request took 196 ms
choices.why: A percentile is not an average; load.py prints no average on purpose.

prompt: A hundred requests take 10 ms each and one takes 2000 ms. What is the average latency, in milliseconds, rounded to the nearest whole number?
hint: Add all 101 times and divide by 101.

prompt: Past the knee of the curve, doubling the workers doubled the median latency and left throughput where it was. What did the extra workers add?

choices.text: Errors, which the latency hides
choices.why: The status line showed only 201s.

choices.text: Length to the queue in front of the processor
choices.why: Right. The box office did no more work; requests waited longer for it.

choices.text: Work for the box office, slowed down by the network
choices.why: Throughput did not rise, so no extra work was done.

choices.text: Load on the database, which became the bottleneck
choices.why: docker stats showed the app at a whole processor and the database at a tenth of one.

prompt: A closed-loop test keeps 32 requests in flight and the system answers 160 a second. About how many milliseconds does each request spend inside it?
hint: Requests inside divided by the rate they leave at.

prompt: During a test, docker stats shows the app at 100.12% and the database at 10.74%. What does that establish?

choices.text: The app is using slightly more than it may, which is an error
choices.why: The extra hundredths are measurement, not a breach of the cap.

choices.text: The app's one processor is the bottleneck
choices.why: Right. It is using all that cpus: 1 allows, while the database has room.

choices.text: nginx is the bottleneck, as it is not listed as busy
choices.why: A bottleneck is the busy resource, not the quiet one.

choices.text: The database is idle and can be removed
choices.why: It holds every ticket; a tenth of a processor is work, not idleness.

prompt: Going from cpus 1 to cpus 2, sales went from 143 to 314 a second, a little more than double. What explains the extra?

choices.text: Measurement error; it was exactly double
choices.why: The capture says 314, which is not 286.

choices.text: Two processors share a cache, which makes each faster
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson measured a cache effect; the cap's behaviour explains it.

choices.text: The one-processor cap pauses a busy container in bursts, and two pauses it less
choices.why: Right. The first number was depressed by the cap itself.

choices.text: The database got faster when the app had more processors
choices.why: The database was not the bottleneck at either size.

prompt: Why did four processors give 433 sales a second rather than about 628?

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits each client to two processors
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no such limit on its clients.

choices.text: Python cannot use more than two processors
choices.why: sign() lets other threads run, and the step from one to two already used both.

choices.text: The machine has four, and the load generator, nginx and the database need some too
choices.why: Right. nproc printed 4; the box office was competing for them.

choices.text: docker update applies only half of the processors it is asked for, to protect the rest of the machine
choices.why: It applied the cap; the machine could not supply it.

prompt: Which of these are limits of vertical scaling named in the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Price that grows faster than size near the top
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The program must be made stateless first
choices.why: That is horizontal scaling's requirement; vertical asks nothing of the program.

choices.text: The largest machine anybody sells
choices.why: Right. Past it there is nothing to buy.

choices.text: One machine is one failure
choices.why: Right. A bigger one is a bigger thing to lose.

prompt: After docker compose up -d --scale app=3, why does the lesson restart lb?

choices.text: Because scaling stops every container
choices.why: The capture shows the others Running throughout.

choices.text: nginx resolves the name app when it starts, and would keep sending to the one address it found
choices.why: Right. The restart makes it look the name up again and see three.

choices.text: To clear its cache of responses
choices.why: This nginx caches nothing.

choices.text: To publish port 8080 again
choices.why: The port was never unpublished.

prompt: Which change would stop the box office from scaling horizontally the way it did?

choices.text: Adding an index to the tickets table
choices.why: The index lives in the database, which every copy shares.

choices.text: Keeping each user's cart in a Python dictionary inside app.py
choices.why: Right. The next request may reach a copy that has never seen that cart.

choices.text: Running nginx with two worker processes
choices.why: That changes nginx, not whether copies of the app are interchangeable.

choices.text: Raising the signing cost to 20,000 rounds, which doubles the processor time of every sale
choices.why: Each sale gets slower, and copies still divide the sales.

prompt: A team keeps sessions in memory and turns on sticky sessions so each user always reaches the same copy. One copy crashes. What do its users see?

choices.text: Slower answers until the copy restarts with their sessions
choices.why: Memory does not survive a crash; the sessions are gone.

choices.text: A 502 on every request from then on
choices.why: The balancer sends them to another copy, which answers, without their session.

choices.text: They are logged out, because their sessions died with the copy
choices.why: Right. Sticky sessions hide the state; they do not share it.

choices.text: Nothing; the load balancer moves their sessions
choices.why: The balancer routes requests; it never had the sessions.

prompt: Match each piece of state to the place it has to live for the copies to stay interchangeable.

pairs.right: the database or a shared cache

prompt: Selling only show 1, three copies sold 138 a second and one copy sold 137. Why did the copies not help?

choices.text: Every sale waits for the lock on show 1's row, held during sign()
choices.why: Right. pg_stat_activity showed fifteen connections waiting on a Lock.

choices.text: Three copies use up the machine's processors
choices.why: The same three copies sold 470 across a hundred shows.

choices.text: nginx sends every request for one show to the same copy
choices.why: It uses round robin, which ignores the path.

choices.text: Show 1 was nearly sold out
choices.why: It has a million seats; every answer was a 201.

prompt: If each sale of one show holds that show's row for 5 ms, what is the most sales of that show per second, whatever the number of copies?
hint: One at a time, 5 ms each.

prompt: Would a machine with twice as many processors raise the sales of the single hot show much?

choices.text: Yes, because PostgreSQL would take and release its locks faster on processors that are less busy
choices.why: Taking the lock is not the cost; holding it is.

choices.text: Yes, it would double them, as vertical scaling did before
choices.why: Earlier the processor was the bottleneck; here the row is.

choices.text: No; the work is waiting for its turn on the row, not for a processor
choices.why: Right. Only a faster sign() would shorten the hold, and only a little.

choices.text: No, because PostgreSQL can only use one processor
choices.why: PostgreSQL runs a process per connection and uses many processors.

prompt: A show's one counter is replaced by ten counters, each owning a tenth of the seats. What gets harder?

choices.text: Saying how many seats are left, which is now a sum
choices.why: Right, and the last seats end up scattered across counters.

choices.text: Preventing the same seat from being sold twice when two sales reach two different counters
choices.why: Each counter still locks its own row; each seat belongs to one counter.

choices.text: Running more than one copy of the box office
choices.why: The copies are as interchangeable as before.

choices.text: Selling two tickets at the same moment
choices.why: That gets easier: two sales can lock two different rows.

prompt: In pg_stat_activity, the hot-row test showed fifteen connections with a wait_event_type of ___.
By Amdahl's law, what is the highest speed-up a request that is 90% parallel can ever reach, on any number of processors?
What does the Universal Scalability Law add to Amdahl's law?

choices.text: The serial fraction, which Amdahl's law leaves out
choices.why: The serial fraction is Amdahl's law.

choices.text: A cost of coordination that grows with the pairs of copies, so throughput peaks and then falls
choices.why: Right. Amdahl only flattens; the second term bends the curve down.

choices.text: A correction for faster processors
choices.why: Both laws are about the number of processors or copies, not their speed.

choices.text: A guarantee that adding copies never makes things slower
choices.why: It says the opposite: past a peak, adding copies makes things slower.

prompt: Match each part of a growing system to the direction it usually scales in first.

pairs.right: neither; it must be split or held less

prompt: Put the steps of investigating a system that stopped keeping up in the order the lesson followed.
items: Measure throughput and latency at increasing load
Find the knee, where throughput stops rising
Name the bottleneck with a tool that shows what is busy
Give that resource more capacity and measure again
trap: Adding capacity before naming the bottleneck is the guess the lesson warns against.

prompt: A service's throughput stays flat as copies are added, and its database shows most connections waiting on a Lock. What is the next thing to try?

choices.text: Find what the transactions hold the lock for, and hold it for less time
choices.why: Right. The lock is the queue; shortening the hold widens it.

choices.text: Raise the database's connection limit so that the waiting transactions get connections of their own
choices.why: The waiting connections already exist; more would only wait too.

choices.text: Give the database a bigger machine, with twice the processors and memory it has today
choices.why: Waiting for a lock is not waiting for a processor.

choices.text: Add more copies until throughput moves
choices.why: More copies are more waiters for the same lock.

prompt: A request is 75% parallel. By Amdahl's law, what speed-up do 3 copies give? Answer to one decimal place.
Which property did the box office have from its first line that let it scale out with no change?

choices.text: It kept nothing between requests
choices.why: Right. Every fact lived in the database.

choices.text: It was written in Python
choices.why: The language did not matter; where the state lived did.

choices.text: It ran behind nginx from the start
choices.why: nginx divides the work; it cannot make stateful copies interchangeable.

choices.text: It used HTTP/1.1 with connections kept open
choices.why: That made each request cheaper, not the copies interchangeable.
